title: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
paragraphs: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
We call it private. Paul calls it something that can cross a boundary, take advantage of another human being, and bring God Himself into the matter.
There is a sentence our culture has learned to say almost automatically whenever sexual morality becomes uncomfortable:
“What two consenting adults do in private is nobody else’s business.”
It sounds reasonable.
It sounds compassionate.
It sounds like the perfect way to end an argument.
Nobody was forced.
Nobody was physically attacked.
Both people agreed.
So what could possibly be wrong?
Then the apostle Paul writes one sentence that refuses to let the conversation remain that simple.
In the middle of one of the New Testament’s clearest passages about sexual holiness, Paul says:
“that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:6
Read that again.
Not merely:
“Do not hurt yourself.”
Not merely:
“Do not break a religious rule.”
Not merely:
“Try to avoid feeling guilty afterward.”
Paul introduces another person.
Someone can be wronged.
And suddenly sexual sin is no longer only about what two people wanted in a moment.
It becomes a question of what one human being may have taken from another.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us have spent years calling something “love” that Scripture may force us to examine as something much more complicated.
Paul originally wrote these words in Greek:
“τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐν τῷ πράγματι τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ…”
The words deserve our attention.
ὑπερβαίνειν — hyperbainein
It carries the idea of stepping beyond, going beyond a boundary, transgressing.
Then comes:
πλεονεκτεῖν — pleonektein
To overreach.
To gain an advantage.
To exploit.
To take advantage of another.
Paul is describing conduct that does not merely happen with another person.
It can happen against another person.
And that changes the question.
The modern question is often:
“Did we both want it?”
Paul forces a deeper question:
“Did I honor this person before God?”
Those are not necessarily the same question.
Because two people can mutually agree to something and still mutually participate in something destructive.
Two people can consent to bitterness.
Two people can cooperate in dishonesty.
Two people can encourage one another toward drunkenness.
Two people can participate willingly in adultery.
Mutual willingness does not automatically transform everything people choose into righteousness.
Biblical love asks something deeper than:
“Will you let me?”
Biblical love asks:
“Will this help me honor you as someone who belongs to God?”
And perhaps that is the question many of us never asked.
We asked whether they wanted us.
We asked whether there was chemistry.
We asked whether anyone would discover it.
We asked whether we were technically dating.
We asked whether everybody else was doing it.
We asked how far was “too far.”
We asked whether God would really care.
But we rarely stopped in the heat of desire and asked:
“Am I helping this person become holy?”
Because lust does not naturally ask that question.
Love does.
And Paul refuses to separate sexuality from holiness.
Listen to the entire movement of his argument:
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:3
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
It is a broad New Testament term for sexual immorality—sexual behavior outside the boundaries God establishes for sexual faithfulness.
Paul continues by telling believers to live in holiness and honor rather than being ruled by “the passion of lust.”
Then comes verse 6.
Do not cross the boundary.
Do not take advantage of your brother or sister “in this matter.”
Then Paul says something even heavier:
“because the Lord is an avenger in all these things…”
This is not casual language.
And yet we need to read it carefully.

There has been interpretive discussion over precisely how Paul’s wording in verse 6 should be understood, particularly the expression ἐν τῷ πράγματι — en tō pragmati, “in the matter.” But the immediate passage unmistakably moves through sanctification, sexual immorality, bodily holiness, lust, wrongdoing toward another person, impurity, holiness, and the Holy Spirit.
So whatever excuses we bring to the text, we cannot honestly pretend Paul thinks sexual conduct is spiritually insignificant.
He does not.
Sex matters because people matter.
Bodies matter because people bearing God’s image matter.
Holiness matters because God matters.
And suddenly another uncomfortable possibility emerges.
Maybe sexual sin sometimes takes something even when the other person willingly gives it.
Maybe you can receive someone’s body while refusing them covenant.
Maybe you can awaken intimacy without accepting responsibility.
Maybe you can whisper permanence while intending something temporary.
Maybe you can enjoy somebody’s vulnerability and disappear when vulnerability becomes inconvenient.
Maybe you can tell yourself, “They wanted it too,” while never asking whether you were leading someone God loves toward holiness or away from it.
And maybe sometimes both people are doing that to each other.
That is what makes sexual sin so deceptive.
It can feel extraordinarily intimate while producing extraordinarily deep loneliness.
Two bodies can be close while two souls remain terrified of being truly known.
Someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You thought giving more of yourself would finally make them stay.
So you crossed another boundary.
Then another.
You told yourself this was what love required.
You were afraid that saying no would mean losing them.
Maybe nobody physically forced you.
But fear was sitting in the room.
Loneliness was sitting in the room.
Insecurity was sitting in the room.
The desperate need to be chosen was sitting in the room.
And afterward…
they still left.
Or perhaps you stayed together, but something changed inside you.
What promised closeness created anxiety.
What promised freedom produced secrecy.
What promised affirmation made you wonder whether you were loved…
or merely desired.
And perhaps you have carried the shame ever since.
But there is another person who needs to keep reading.
The person who did the using.
Maybe you never called it that.
You said:
“We both knew what this was.”
You said:
“They could have said no.”
You said:
“We weren't married.”
You said:
“It was consensual.”
You said:
“I never promised anything.”
Maybe technically, according to the rules you created for yourself, you can construct a defense.
But stand before Jesus for a moment and ask a different question.
Did you love them?
Not:
Did you desire them?
Not:
Did they desire you?
Did you love them with a love that sought their holiness, dignity, spiritual good, and eternal good?
Because Scripture’s definition of love is far more demanding than desire with permission.
Love “does no wrong to a neighbor.”
—Romans 13:10
Love does not ask:
“How much can I take without technically becoming the villain?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor you because Christ died for sinners like both of us?”
That changes everything.
And before anyone turns this article into ammunition against someone else, hear this carefully.
Paul is not giving religious people permission to stand over sexually broken people with stones in their hands.
Christianity begins with the devastating realization that we are the sinners who need mercy.
Sexual sin is real.
But so is sexual shame.
And shame has convinced millions of people that their worst night became their permanent name.
Adulterer.
Porn addict.
Used.
Dirty.
Unfaithful.
Promiscuous.
Unworthy.
Damaged.
Hypocrite.
Maybe nobody knows.
You sing worship songs.
You post Bible verses.
You go to church.
You smile when people ask how you are.
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is a memory you desperately hope never becomes public.
A browser history.
A hotel room.
A message thread.
A relationship nobody knew about.
Someone else's husband.
Someone else's wife.
A secret addiction.
A compromise you promised God would happen only once.
Then twice.
Then again.
And perhaps the hardest part is not merely remembering what someone did to you.
It is remembering what you did to someone else.
That is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people feel spiritually encouraged.
Jesus came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Guilty sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
People who were wronged.
And people who did the wronging.
People whose sexuality was exploited.
And people who selfishly exploited others.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who broke vows.
People who hid.
People who lied.
People who cannot rewind what happened.
The Gospel does not say your sin was harmless.
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
your sin does not have to have the final word.
At the cross, Jesus does not rename darkness as light so we can avoid repentance.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can be forgiven and transformed.
Grace is not God pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God doing for guilty people what guilty people could never do for themselves.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus changes hearts.
And Jesus calls us out of the darkness we once defended.
That is why Paul does not stop at prohibition.
Just one verse later he says:
“For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness.”
—1 Thessalonians 4:7
Called.
Do you see it?
Christian sexual ethics are not merely about what God tells you to run from.
They are about what God is calling you into.
Holiness.
Freedom.
Integrity.
A life where your body no longer controls your master.
A life where another person's body is not something to consume.
A life where desire learns to bow before Jesus.
A life where you stop asking how close you can walk to the cliff and start asking how closely you can walk with Christ.
And then Paul writes:
—1 Thessalonians 4:8
Notice that final phrase.
God gives His Holy Spirit.
Paul does not leave struggling believers standing before an impossible command with nothing but willpower.
God gives Himself.
The Spirit who convicts is also the Spirit who empowers.
So if you have fallen sexually, the answer is not pretending it never mattered.
And the answer is not spending the rest of your life believing you are too filthy for Jesus.
The answer is repentance.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
End what needs ending.
Block what needs blocking.
Flee what needs fleeing.
Seek pastoral or mature Christian accountability where needed.

If you have seriously wronged someone, repentance may involve accepting consequences and seeking wise counsel about appropriate restitution rather than demanding immediate forgiveness or renewed access to the person you hurt.

And where abuse, coercion, assault, exploitation, or criminal conduct has occurred, do not hide it behind vague religious language about “mutual sin.” Victims are not morally responsible for another person's abuse against them, and serious wrongdoing may require professional, pastoral, safeguarding, and legal intervention.
Biblical grace never requires calling evil good.
Grace tells the truth…
and then opens the door home.
Perhaps that is why this message hurts.
You did not expect 1 Thessalonians 4:6 to expose that memory.
You did not expect one Greek verb to make you reconsider a relationship you have spent years justifying.
You did not expect to wonder whether something you called “consensual” was nevertheless selfish.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God.”
Conviction says:
“Come back to God.”
Condemnation says:
“You are what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“There is redemption in Jesus Christ.”
The woman caught in adultery encountered a Savior who neither celebrated her sin nor abandoned her to her accusers.
Grace did not say sin was meaningless.
Grace gave the sinner somewhere to go.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Maybe you have been carrying sexual shame for ten years.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe what happened was last night.
Maybe you are still inside the relationship you know you need to surrender.
Maybe you are reading this beside the person with whom you keep compromising.
Maybe you have confessed the same sin so many times that you are embarrassed to pray again.
Pray anyway.
Run to Christ again.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Repentance means turning.
And sometimes turning begins with one trembling sentence:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
If that is you, do not perform for the comments.

And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you once believed could never be healed, tell someone what grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to give another wounded person enough courage to seek help.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because you need another saved post buried in your phone, but because temptation has an extraordinary ability to make us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Not to publicly shame anyone. Not to throw stones.
Truth should be carried with love.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Give because you freely want to help the work continue.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help enormously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
Invite someone to follow.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your heart while reading.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is calling bondage freedom.
Someone is calling lust love.
Someone is calling shame their identity.
Someone is convinced they have gone too far for Jesus to want them anymore.
And they need to discover what the Gospel has been saying all along.
Sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending.
The night you thought permanently stained your name may become the very place where the mercy of Jesus teaches you what it means to be made new.
